raw:
You finish the last of the stew while Jo gathers the plates nearest her.

“I’ll wash these at home if I have to,” she says, looking at the unopened crockery cartons, “but I’d rather know whether we’ve got enough mugs before I start serving coffee to a queue.”

“We have enough,” Nell says. “I counted this afternoon.”

“Counted, or saw several boxes and developed faith?”

“Counted.”

Jo accepts that with a small nod. “Then I’ll price the opening menu tonight and send it over tomorrow. No printing until I’ve checked what the suppliers are actually charging me.”

“Fine,” Nell says. “I’ll need your opening hours for the programme insert by Wednesday.”

Owen returns from the kitchen with a damp tea towel over one shoulder. “I can help set the café tables out Thursday morning, if that’s useful.”

“It is,” Nell says. “You’re on front-of-house from ten, so make it part of that shift. Don’t arrive early and donate an hour.”

“Wasn’t planning to.”

From behind the auditorium doors comes the faint scrape of something being moved carefully across the floor, then Martin’s muffled voice. No test sound follows it.

Bea comes back into the foyer carrying the pencil Rosa had apparently handed her. She sets it beside the opening programmes. “They’ve started with the blue board. Martin’s being good so far.”

“That’s because I can hear you,” Martin calls from inside.

Bea smiles and sits again, though only briefly. “I’ll stay until they’ve finished. I want to make sure those boards get put back safely.”

Nell closes her clipboard. “I’m locking up the office paperwork in ten minutes, then I’m heading home. Tomorrow: Rowan and I start at nine. Dev, send me Hana’s available times when you have them.”

“Will do,” Dev calls from upstairs.

Owen dries his hands, then looks at Nell. “Could I have two minutes with you before you go?”

Nell glances toward the office. “Of course.”

Jo’s attention stays on the stack of plates as she says, “I’ll finish these. Go on.”

Owen follows Nell into the office. The door closes behind them, leaving the foyer quieter: the soft clink of Jo stacking dishes, Bea turning an opening programme over in her hands, and the work in the auditorium continuing on the other side of its shut doors.
